posts.title: orchestration failures not model failures
posts.hook: Your AI agent isn't failing because the model is bad. It's failing because your orchestration is bad.
posts.body:
Your AI agent isn't failing because the model is bad. It's failing because your orchestration is bad.

I run Claude Code agents across content, GTM, and website builds every day. The model almost never gets it wrong in ways that matter. What gets it wrong:

- Context windows that bloat past usefulness
- No memory between sessions, so every run starts from zero
- Instructions that contradict each other across three config files
- Subagents spawned without clear scope, spinning in loops

The fix isn't a better model. The fix is treating your agent like infrastructure.

I keep a CLAUDE.md file that's basically a runbook. Session handoffs so the next run picks up where the last one left off. Skill files that route tasks to the right workflow. A lessons.md that the agent reads on startup so it doesn't repeat mistakes.

None of this is fancy. It's the same stuff you'd do for a junior engineer on their first week. Clear instructions, documented context, feedback loops.

The teams shipping real agent workflows aren't prompt engineering wizards. They're the ones who treat orchestration as a first-class engineering problem.

remixes.label: infrastructure-not-intelligence
remixes.hook: Stop blaming GPT-4 for your broken agent. The model is the least interesting part of the stack.
remixes.body:
Stop blaming GPT-4 for your broken agent. The model is the least interesting part of the stack.

I ship agent workflows daily. Content pipelines, GTM automation, website builds. After hundreds of sessions, I can tell you the failure pattern is almost never "the model hallucinated" or "it couldn't reason."

The failure pattern is plumbing.

Session A writes a file. Session B doesn't know it exists. An agent gets a 200k-token context window stuffed with irrelevant history and starts making bizarre decisions. Two instruction files contradict each other and the agent picks the wrong one.

These aren't model problems. They're infrastructure problems. And they're boring to fix, which is exactly why most people don't fix them.

What actually works: explicit memory systems between sessions. Context windows that get pruned, not just appended to. Instruction hierarchies where one file wins when two conflict. File structures the agent can navigate without searching the entire repo.

The teams shipping real agent workflows aren't using better models. They're building better scaffolding around the same models everyone else has access to.

The model is a commodity. The orchestration is the product.

remixes.label: context-engineering-over-prompt-engineering
remixes.hook: Prompt engineering is a skill ceiling. Context engineering is the actual job.
remixes.body:
Prompt engineering is a skill ceiling. Context engineering is the actual job.

Everyone obsesses over the perfect prompt. The right system message. The magic words that make the model perform.

Meanwhile, the agents that actually ship code and produce real output? They run on boring context management.

I learned this by running Claude Code across my entire operation. Same model, same prompts, wildly different outcomes depending on one thing: what context was loaded when the agent started working.

A session with the right CLAUDE.md, the right handoff doc from yesterday, and a clean context window finishes a feature in one pass. The same session with a bloated window and no prior state burns 30 minutes going in circles before producing something half-baked.

The difference isn't the prompt. It's what the agent knows before you even ask it to do anything.

Context engineering means: designing what information is available, when it loads, how much of it fits, and what gets discarded. It means treating the agent's working memory as a system you architect, not a text box you paste into.

This is the real skill gap right now. Not who writes the best prompts. Who builds the best context pipelines.
remixes.cta: How do you manage context across agent sessions? Or are you still starting from scratch every time?

posts.title: agent billing is broken
posts.hook: SaaS pricing was built for humans clicking buttons. Agents don't click buttons.
posts.body:
SaaS pricing was built for humans clicking buttons. Agents don't click buttons.

I watch this play out in my own stack. My agents hit Apollo for enrichment, Exa for web research, Attio for CRM writes, Typefully for publishing. Every one of those tools prices per seat or per month with usage caps designed for a person working 8 hours a day.

An agent works 24 hours a day and makes 200 API calls in a 10-minute session.

The tools that get this right will win the next era of B2B. The ones that don't will get replaced by a Python script and an API key.

I've already replaced three tools this year with scripts that cost me pennies per run. Not because the tools were bad. Because their pricing assumed a human operator and my operator is Claude.

The pattern I'm seeing: every tool that charges per seat is vulnerable. Every tool that charges per outcome or per API call has a future. The consumption model isn't just a pricing trend. It's the only model that makes sense when your "user" is an autonomous agent burning through 10x the volume of a human.

Founders building infra right now should be pricing for agents, not people.
posts.cta: Which tools in your stack would break if an agent used them at full speed?

remixes.label: per-seat-pricing-extinction
remixes.hook: Per-seat SaaS pricing has maybe 18 months left. Most vendors haven't figured that out yet.
remixes.body:
Per-seat SaaS pricing has maybe 18 months left. Most vendors haven't figured that out yet.

Here's the math that breaks it. I run agents that hit my CRM, enrichment tools, web research APIs, and publishing platforms. Each agent makes more API calls in an hour than I make in a week. But it's not a "seat." It doesn't have a login. It doesn't take lunch breaks.

So what happens when I point an agent at a tool built for human usage patterns?

Rate limits hit within minutes. Monthly quotas burn in days. I'm paying for a plan designed for one person clicking buttons 8 hours a day, but consuming like 10 people working around the clock.

The vendors who figure this out first will win the next wave. Outcome-based pricing. Per-action metering. Tiered API access that scales with machine consumption patterns instead of fighting them.

The vendors who don't will watch their best customers churn. Not because the product is bad, but because the pricing model punishes the exact behavior their customers are adopting.

Every SaaS company right now should be modeling what happens to their unit economics when 30% of their usage comes from agents instead of humans. Most haven't started.
remixes.cta: Which SaaS tool in your stack is most vulnerable to agent-driven consumption blowing up the pricing model?

remixes.label: agent-arbitrage
remixes.hook: I accidentally spent $400 in API credits in one weekend because my agent didn't know what things cost.
remixes.body:
I accidentally spent $400 in API credits in one weekend because my agent didn't know what things cost.

My enrichment agent was running a standard prospecting workflow. Find companies, enrich contacts, verify emails, push to CRM. Normal stuff.

Except it was making enrichment calls on contacts it had already enriched in a previous session. It was re-verifying emails that were verified two days ago. It had no concept of "I already paid for this data."

This is the billing problem nobody talks about with agents. It's not just that SaaS pricing doesn't fit machine consumption. It's that agents have zero cost awareness.

A human looks at a credit balance and self-regulates. An agent burns through credits the same way it burns through tokens. As fast as possible, with no concept of diminishing returns.

So now I build cost guards into every workflow. Cache enrichment results locally so we never pay twice for the same data. Set hard budget caps per session. Log every API call with its cost so I can audit spend per workflow.

The agent doesn't care about your budget. You have to build the caring into the system.

This is going to become a real category. Agent cost management. Right now it's just me writing SQLite queries. In a year, someone will raise a Series A on it.

posts.title: vibe coding ceiling
posts.hook: Vibe coding gets you to 80% in 20 minutes. The last 20% takes longer than if you'd written it by hand.
posts.body:
Vibe coding gets you to 80% in 20 minutes. The last 20% takes longer than if you'd written it by hand.

I say this as someone who builds almost everything with Claude Code now. Websites, scripts, data pipelines, content systems. The agent writes most of the code.

But here's what I've learned the hard way: if you can't read the code it generates, you can't debug it. And you will need to debug it.

Last week my content dispatch pipeline broke silently. Posts were getting approved but not sent. The agent had written a clean async handler that looked perfect. The bug was a race condition in how Discord webhooks got queued. Took me 45 minutes to find because I had to actually understand the control flow, not just prompt my way through it.

The developers shipping real products with AI aren't the ones who prompt the fastest. They're the ones who can read a stack trace, understand what the agent built, and fix the thing it missed.

Vibe coding is a superpower when you already know how to code. It's a trap when you don't. The gap between "it works in dev" and "it works in production" is still made of fundamentals.

Learn to read before you learn to prompt.

remixes.label: illiteracy-tax
remixes.hook: Vibe coding creates a new kind of technical debt: code you shipped but can't read.
remixes.body:
Vibe coding creates a new kind of technical debt: code you shipped but can't read.

Traditional tech debt is code you understand but chose to write poorly. Time pressure, shortcuts, things you plan to refactor later.

Vibe coding debt is different. It's code that works, that you deployed, that serves real users. And you have no idea how it works.

I build almost everything with Claude Code now. It writes most of the code. But I can read every line it generates because I could have written it myself, just slower.

That's the distinction people miss. The agent isn't replacing the skill of writing code. It's accelerating it. If you don't have the underlying skill, you're not accelerating anything. You're accumulating mystery code.

And mystery code is fine until something breaks. Then you're staring at a function you don't understand, in a framework you've never used, trying to debug logic you didn't write and can't trace.

The fix isn't "don't use AI coding tools." The fix is: learn to read code at the same speed you learn to generate it. Treat the AI output like a pull request from a junior dev. Review it. Understand it. Then ship it.

If you skip the review step, you're not coding faster. You're building a system you'll eventually lose control of.
remixes.cta: What's your review process for AI-generated code? Or do you ship and hope?

remixes.label: 80-percent-trap
remixes.hook: The 80% that AI coding gives you for free is the easy 80%. The hard 20% is where the actual engineering lives.
remixes.body:
The 80% that AI coding gives you for free is the easy 80%. The hard 20% is where the actual engineering lives.

Scaffolding a Next.js app. Wiring up a database schema. Building CRUD endpoints. Generating component boilerplate. All of this is trivial for an AI coding agent. And all of it was already the least interesting part of building software.

The interesting part. The part that determines whether your product works in production. That's error handling for edge cases the agent never considered. Performance under real load. Security for attack vectors that don't show up in happy-path testing. State management when three systems disagree about the truth.

This is the work that AI coding tools punt on. Not because the models can't do it, but because these problems require understanding the full system in context. And context is exactly what gets lost when you're generating code file by file.

So yes, vibe coding gets you to a working prototype absurdly fast. But the distance between "working prototype" and "production system" is where engineering judgment lives. And that judgment comes from experience debugging, not experience prompting.

The people who will thrive with AI coding tools are the ones who already know what good code looks like. Everyone else is building sandcastles.

posts.title: what separates agents that close PRs
posts.hook: The difference between an AI coding agent that ships and one that spins in loops is boring. It's file structure.
posts.body:
The difference between an AI coding agent that ships and one that spins in loops is boring. It's file structure.

I've been running Claude Code as my primary dev tool for months. The sessions where it nails a feature in one pass vs. the ones where it burns tokens going in circles come down to three things:

1. A CLAUDE.md that tells it exactly where things live, what conventions to follow, and what not to touch
2. Skill files that break complex workflows into discrete, testable steps
3. A todo system where it checks off items as it goes instead of trying to hold the whole plan in context

That's it. No custom frameworks. No fine-tuning. Just... good project organization.

The same agent, same model, same temperature will either close a PR cleanly or loop for 20 minutes depending on whether your repo has clear entry points and documented conventions.

This tracks with what I saw managing junior engineers years ago. The codebase that was well-organized made everyone faster. The messy one made everyone slower. The talent was the same. The environment changed the output.

If your agent keeps spinning, don't blame the model. Clean up your repo.

remixes.label: agent-mise-en-place
remixes.hook: A chef doesn't cook faster by turning up the heat. They cook faster because everything is in the right place before they start.
remixes.body:
A chef doesn't cook faster by turning up the heat. They cook faster because everything is in the right place before they start.

Same principle applies to AI coding agents.

I've been running Claude Code as my primary dev tool for months. And the single biggest predictor of whether a session ships clean code or burns tokens in circles is mise en place. The prep work before the agent starts.

A CLAUDE.md file that maps the codebase. Where things live. What conventions to follow. What not to touch. This is the recipe card.

A context handoff from the previous session. What was built, what broke, what's next. This is the prep list.

Clean file structure with predictable naming. So the agent can navigate without searching the entire repo every time it needs to find something. This is the organized station.

None of this is glamorous. None of it involves better prompts or smarter models. It's just preparation.

posts.title: reply rate is a vanity metric
posts.hook: A 12% reply rate means nothing if 80% of those replies are "not interested" or "wrong person."
posts.body:
A 12% reply rate means nothing if 80% of those replies are "not interested" or "wrong person."

I track everything from enrichment to booked meeting in a single SQLite database. No Salesforce dashboards. No BI tool. Just SQL queries against raw pipeline data.

What I found when I started measuring meeting-to-pipeline instead of reply rate:

- Campaigns with lower reply rates but tighter targeting converted 3x better
- The "personalized" subject line tests everyone runs barely moved the needle on actual pipeline
- Signal-based timing (job changes, funding, tech installs) mattered more than any copy variation

The outbound teams still optimizing for reply rate are optimizing for a proxy metric that doesn't correlate with revenue the way they think it does.

The play: measure from the other end. Start with closed-won deals, trace backwards to what sourced them, and build more of that. Most teams do the opposite. They start with sends, optimize forward, and wonder why pipeline doesn't grow.

Reply rate is the outbound equivalent of "time on page" in content marketing. It feels important. It measures activity, not outcomes.

I replaced our entire outbound analytics stack with a single SQLite database and raw SQL. The insights got better.

No Salesforce. No HubSpot dashboards. No BI tool. Just every enrichment call, every email sent, every reply, every meeting booked, every deal, tracked in one local database.

Why this works better than the traditional stack:

I can query across the entire funnel in one statement. "Show me the campaigns where reply rate was below average but meeting rate was above average." That query takes 3 seconds in SQL. It takes 20 minutes of clicking through dashboard filters in a CRM.

I can track metrics that CRMs don't surface. Cost per enrichment call that actually led to a booked meeting. Time between first touch and reply by persona. Which enrichment source produced contacts that converted vs. contacts that bounced.

And I can spot the metric that actually matters: meeting-to-pipeline conversion. Not open rate. Not reply rate. Not even meeting rate. The rate at which meetings turn into real pipeline.

When I started measuring that instead of reply rate, everything changed. The campaigns I thought were winning were actually producing low-quality conversations. The "boring" campaigns with modest reply rates were booking meetings that closed.

Reply rate is a vanity metric that makes you feel productive while your pipeline stays empty.

I cut our outbound volume by 60% and booked more meetings. The math is obvious in retrospect.

We were optimizing for reply rate. More replies meant better campaigns, right? So we wrote hooks designed to provoke responses. We targeted broadly to increase volume. We measured success by how many people wrote back.

80% of those replies were "not interested," "wrong person," or "remove me." Technically replies. Practically worthless.

When I switched to measuring meeting-to-pipeline, the whole strategy inverted.

Tighter targeting. Fewer sends. Higher relevance per email. The reply rate dropped from 12% to 7%. But the meetings-booked rate tripled. And those meetings converted to pipeline at 3x the rate of the old high-reply campaigns.

The insight: reply rate rewards provocation. Meeting rate rewards relevance. Pipeline rate rewards targeting. These are three different optimization functions and most outbound teams are optimizing for the wrong one.

I track all of this in a single SQLite database. Every touchpoint from enrichment to closed deal. No dashboard abstraction layer hiding the truth behind pretty charts.

Raw data tells you what's working. Dashboards tell you what looks like it's working. Those are very different things.

If you're celebrating a high reply rate, go count how many of those replies turned into pipeline. The number might surprise you.

posts.title: revops is stuck maintaining not building
posts.hook: Most RevOps teams spend 70% of their time maintaining Salesforce and 30% doing actual operations work. That ratio is backwards.
posts.body:
Most RevOps teams spend 70% of their time maintaining Salesforce and 30% doing actual operations work. That ratio is backwards.

I see this pattern constantly with GTM teams I work with. The RevOps person is the most technical person on the go-to-market side. They understand data, systems, workflows. And they're spending their days fixing broken Salesforce automations, deduplicating records, and building reports nobody reads.

The shift: treat RevOps like engineering.

I run my entire GTM operation from SQLite + Python scripts + Claude Code. Enrichment pipelines, lead scoring, campaign tracking, analytics. All version-controlled. All reproducible. All debuggable with a stack trace instead of clicking through Salesforce setup menus.

Not saying everyone should ditch Salesforce. But the RevOps teams creating real leverage are the ones building programmatic infrastructure alongside their CRM, not inside it.

A Python script that enriches, scores, and routes leads takes an afternoon to build. The equivalent Salesforce flow takes a week, breaks silently, and requires a certified admin to modify.

The best RevOps people I know are becoming GTM engineers. They're writing code, not configuring tools.

What if you gave them one day a week with zero maintenance tickets? Just building. New scoring models, new routing logic, new pipeline analytics, new integrations that eliminate the manual work that eats the other four days.

posts.title: linkedin virality vs substance
posts.hook: The LinkedIn post that got me the most impressions last month taught nothing. The one that got me the most inbound had 1/10th the reach.

The LinkedIn post that got me the most impressions last month taught nothing. The one that got me the most inbound had 1/10th the reach.

posts.title: solo founder revenue transparency
posts.hook: I don't post Stripe screenshots. I post the systems that generate the revenue.
posts.body:
I don't post Stripe screenshots. I post the systems that generate the revenue.

I've noticed a pattern in the build-in-public space. Revenue screenshots get massive engagement. The actual build decisions that created that revenue get ignored.

But the decisions are the valuable part.

Decisions like:

- Running my entire content pipeline through Claude Code instead of hiring a content team
- Building enrichment scripts that cost $0.003 per lead instead of paying $15k/year for a point tool
- Using SQLite as my CRM instead of Salesforce, because I need queryable data, not a UI
- Spending 2 hours building a Reddit intent scanner instead of paying for a buyer intent platform

Each of those saved money or created leverage. None of them look impressive in a screenshot.

The solo founders actually building sustainable businesses aren't the ones flexing MRR charts. They're the ones making boring infrastructure decisions that compound over months.

A $5k MRR screenshot tells you nothing about whether that revenue is sustainable, what the margins look like, or whether the founder is working 80 hours a week to maintain it.

The system behind the number is the story worth telling.

I see founders post MRR screenshots every week. $10K month. $50K month. $100K month. Massive engagement. Everyone claps.

But nobody asks the question that matters: what system produced this?

Because the system is the replicable part. The revenue number is the output. You can't reverse-engineer a business from its outputs.

Here's what I post instead. The decisions.

I run my entire content pipeline through Claude Code instead of hiring a content team. That's not a flex. It's an infrastructure choice that keeps my content costs near zero while producing daily across four platforms.

I built my outbound pipeline with agents and Email Bison instead of using Instantly or Smartlead. That means I control the sending infrastructure, the warm-up schedule, the data flow. No vendor lock-in, no monthly seat cost scaling with volume.

I chose Attio over Salesforce for CRM. Not because it's cheaper. Because the API-first design means my agent workflows can read and write to it without fighting the platform.

None of these decisions photograph well. They don't get reshared. But they're the reason the revenue exists.

The builders I learn the most from share the boring architectural choices, not the shiny outputs.

Tuesday: rewrote my cold email sending logic because Email Bison's retry behavior wasn't matching what I expected. Shipped the fix. No one noticed.

Wednesday: realized my content pipeline had a silent failure mode where posts would get generated but never dispatched. Found it by accident while checking something else.

Thursday: had a call with a prospect who found me through a Reddit comment I made three weeks ago. The comment took 2 minutes to write.

None of this makes a good Stripe screenshot. All of it is how the business actually works.

The build-in-public community has accidentally created a format where the only acceptable content is the after photo. Revenue up. Users up. Launch day.

But the before and during is where the learning happens. The debug sessions, the infrastructure decisions, the quiet fixes that prevent future problems.

I'd rather follow a founder who posts their Wednesday bug fix than their Friday revenue screenshot. The bug fix teaches me something. The screenshot just tells me they have Stripe.

posts.title: when the runway gets real
posts.hook: 60 days of runway changes what you're willing to build.
posts.body:
60 days of runway changes what you're willing to build.

Not from a startup. From going independent.

When I left my last role, I had savings and a plan. The plan was to build Clearbox, a Reddit opportunity inbox, and monetize within 90 days. Clean, linear, founder-brained.

Reality: the first version took 6 weeks. Revenue took longer. The gap between "this works" and "someone will pay for this" was wider than I expected.

What short runway actually taught me:

- Kill features fast. If it doesn't connect to revenue in the next 30 days, it doesn't exist.
- Build with agents, not engineers. My entire stack runs on Claude Code because I can't afford a team and don't need one.
- Ship the system, not the product. Clearbox isn't a SaaS app with a login page. It's a pipeline that delivers qualified Reddit threads to my inbox. The "product" is the output, not the wrapper.
- Revenue comes from services first. Every product founder I know funded their product with consulting. I'm no different.

Short runway doesn't kill companies. Building the wrong thing on short runway kills companies.

The constraint forced clarity. I'd take that trade again.
posts.cta: For the founders running lean: what constraint ended up being the thing that focused you?

I planned for 90 days. Revenue took longer. That gap taught me more than any startup playbook.

When I went independent, I had a clean plan. Build Clearbox. Ship a Reddit opportunity inbox. Monetize in 90 days. The timeline felt generous.

The first version took 6 weeks. But "works" and "someone will pay for this" are separated by a canyon that no one talks about. The product worked. The positioning didn't. The audience wasn't ready. The pricing was wrong.

So I did what runway pressure forces you to do: I stopped building features and started talking to people. Every conversation narrowed the focus. Every "not right now" taught me what "right now" actually looks like for my buyer.

The constraint didn't just focus me. It forced me to prioritize revenue-generating activities over product-building activities. Those feel like the same thing when you're a builder. They are absolutely not.

I stopped adding features to Clearbox and started doing GTM engineering consulting on the side. The consulting revealed the exact pain points that eventually made the product sell. The constraint created the feedback loop I would have never designed on purpose.

Short runway doesn't kill good ideas. It kills the luxury of building in isolation. And building in isolation is where most solo founder projects go to die quietly.

The product worked on day 42. Someone paid for it on day 127. Nobody warns you about that gap.

Every founder story I read before going independent followed the same arc. Build the thing, launch it, get customers. Maybe a rough week or two in between. The timeline was always compressed in the retelling.

Real timeline: 6 weeks to build Clearbox. Then weeks of "this is cool but not what I need right now." Then pivoting the positioning. Then adjusting the pricing. Then finding the actual buyer persona, which was different from who I assumed.

During that gap, runway is burning. And the burning changes what you pay attention to. When you have 12 months, you can afford to optimize the product. When you have 60 days, you optimize for the conversation that leads to a check.

That shift in attention is where most of the learning happens. Not in the code. In the sales calls that don't convert. In the positioning experiments that fall flat. In the pricing conversations that reveal what your buyer actually values.

I wouldn't romanticize the stress. But I would say this: the founder who ships on a short timeline builds a fundamentally different product than the one with comfortable runway. Not better or worse. More honest about what the market wants.

The gap between "works" and "pays" is where the business gets built. The product is just the prerequisite.

You stop adding features. You start having conversations. The constraint kills isolation, and isolation is where most solo products go to die.

platforms.newsletter:
When I went independent, I had a clean 90-day plan. Build the product, launch it, monetize. It didn't go that way.

The build took 6 weeks. Revenue took much longer. And that gap, the one between "this works" and "someone will pay for this," is something nobody talks about honestly.

This week I want to share what that gap actually looked like, and why the runway constraint turned out to be the most useful forcing function I didn't plan for.
